dialogue.english: There are many clouds, so it might rain this evening.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Kune [to / at ne] • makore [plural kore] • akawanda [he/she (past) wanda] • saka [so / therefore] • kunogona [to / at nogona] • kungonaya [to / at ngonaya] • manheru [good evening / evening]

grammar_notes.title: Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('manheru')
grammar_notes.content: In this lesson you encounter 'manheru'. Shona greetings change depending on the time of day and how many people you are addressing. 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, 'Masikati' in the afternoon, and 'Manheru' in the evening. For a casual 'Hello' to a friend or peer, use 'Mhoro' (or 'Mhoroi' when speaking politely to an elder or group). To ask 'How are you?', speakers use 'Makadini?' (polite/plural) or ask how your day went with 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?').
grammar_notes.rule: Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akawanda')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akawanda' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('kunogona')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'kunogona' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: Reading Evening Storm Clouds ('Makore') on the Highveld
cultural_notes.content: During the rainy season ('zhizha'), towering cumulus clouds ('makore akawanda') build up across the central Zimbabwean plateau through the warm afternoon before releasing dramatic late-afternoon or evening downpours ('kunaya manheru').
